title: HE REFUSED TO KILL HIS ENEMY—BUT WAS HE DISOBEYING HIS COUNTRY OR OBEYING JESUS?
paragraphs: HE REFUSED TO KILL HIS ENEMY—BUT WAS HE DISOBEYING HIS COUNTRY OR OBEYING JESUS?
When the Government Demands a Weapon, but Christ Commands Love: The Christian Conscience, Military Service, and the Cost of Following Jesus
Imagine standing before a military officer.
Your country is calling you to serve. Your family expects you to be brave. Your neighbors believe that defending your nation is your sacred duty.
Then someone places a weapon in your hands.
You know what that weapon is designed to do.
And somewhere deep inside, a voice you cannot silence brings back the words of Jesus Christ:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
Your hands begin to tremble.
Not necessarily because you are afraid to die.
But because you are afraid of taking a life that God created.
Now imagine the officer looking straight into your eyes and asking:
“Are you refusing to serve your country?”
And you answer:

“Sir, I am willing to suffer for my country. I am willing to carry the wounded. I am willing to risk my life to save another human being. But I cannot, in good conscience, take a life when I believe my Savior is calling me to love even my enemies.”
Silence.
Then comes the accusation.
“Coward.”
“Traitor.”
“Disobedient.”
“Fake patriot.”
Perhaps even the accusation that hurts most:
“You call yourself a Christian, but you refuse to defend the innocent?”
And suddenly, this is no longer a simple question about military service.
It is a question about the authority of Jesus Christ over the human conscience.
Can a Christian refuse military service because Jesus commanded His followers to love their enemies?
Yes, a Christian can sincerely refuse participation in military service, especially combat, because of a conscience shaped by Jesus' teachings.
But that is not the end of the biblical discussion.
Because Scripture also speaks about governing authorities, soldiers, justice, protecting others, and the moral responsibility to resist evil.
And faithful Christians have wrestled with these passages for centuries.
The deeper question is not whether we can find one Bible verse that supports our preferred position.

The deeper question is whether we are willing to let the whole counsel of God examine our hearts—even when it challenges our patriotism, our fear, our politics, or our understanding of what courage really means.
Because a person can refuse to carry a weapon for selfish reasons.
And another person can carry a weapon while sincerely believing he is protecting innocent lives.
The weapon alone does not reveal everything about the heart.
And the absence of a weapon does not automatically prove holiness.
Jesus sees deeper.
Much deeper.
The words that disturbed an empire
When Jesus delivered His Sermon on the Mount, He did not tell His disciples merely to avoid hating their enemies.
He commanded something far more radical.
In Matthew 5:44, the Greek text reads:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn.
“Love your enemies.”
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is an imperative from agapaō, meaning to love. Here, Jesus commands His followers to love those who stand against them.
And ἐχθρούς (echthrous) refers to enemies.
Not merely people who irritate us.
Not merely people who disagree with our opinions.
Enemies.
People who oppose us.
People who may threaten us.
People whose actions make loving them painfully difficult.
Jesus continues in Matthew 5:45:
“That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
Think about that.
The God who has every right to judge wickedness still extends ordinary gifts of providence to people who reject Him.
And Jesus commands His followers to reflect the character of that Father.
This does not mean that evil is harmless.
It does not mean injustice should be ignored.
It does not mean victims must remain defenseless.
But it does mean that a Christian must never treat another human being as someone beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Even an enemy remains a person made in God's image.
Even an enemy may become a recipient of God's saving grace.
And this is where the Christian conscience begins to wrestle.
If Jesus commands me to love my enemy, can I deliberately take his life in battle?
Some Christians answer no.
Others believe that love for an enemy can coexist with the tragic necessity of using proportionate force to protect innocent people.
Both positions deserve careful examination against Scripture.
But neither position gives us permission to hate.
The moment Jesus refused the sword
Now travel in your imagination to the Garden of Gethsemane.
It is night.
Torches approach through the darkness.
Judas has betrayed the Son of God.
Armed men arrive to arrest the only truly innocent man who has ever lived.
Peter sees the danger.
He reaches for his sword.
Steel flashes.
A servant of the high priest loses his ear.
And Jesus says something Peter probably never expected.
“Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.” — Matthew 26:52 (KJV)
Luke 22:51 records that Jesus healed the wounded man's ear.
Consider the scene.
The man who had come with the arresting party was wounded.
Jesus did not celebrate his suffering.
He healed him.
The Savior was surrounded by hostility, yet His response revealed the extraordinary mercy of His kingdom.
But we must be careful not to make the passage say more—or less—than it says.
Jesus was preventing His disciples from violently resisting His arrest. He was willingly fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
The passage does not explicitly declare that every soldier in every circumstance must abandon military service.
Nevertheless, Christian pacifists see in this moment a profound revelation of how disciples are called to respond to violence.
Jesus did not establish His kingdom through the sword.
He went to the cross.
And there, while suffering at the hands of His enemies, He prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)
This is not weakness.
This is holiness.
This is not cowardice.
This is the Son of God refusing to abandon love even while enduring unimaginable injustice.
And anyone who claims to follow Him must take that example seriously.
But what about the soldiers in the Bible?
Here is where the discussion becomes more difficult.
Because the same Bible that records Jesus commanding love for enemies also records encounters with soldiers without always demanding that they leave their profession.
In Luke 3:14, soldiers asked John the Baptist what they should do.
John answered:
“Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.” (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “Do violence to no man” is:
Μηδένα διασείσητε
Mēdena diaseisēte.
The verb diaseiō can refer to intimidating, shaking down, or extorting someone through threats or force.
John was condemning the abuse of military authority.
He also warned against false accusations and greed.
Significantly, he did not explicitly command those soldiers to resign.
That observation matters.
However, it would also be a mistake to claim that John's silence settles every question about warfare or killing.
The passage directly addresses the conduct of soldiers, not every moral question about military service.
Then consider the Roman centurion in Matthew 8.
Jesus praised his faith.
He did not explicitly demand that he abandon his military position.
In Acts 10, Cornelius, another centurion, is described as devout and God-fearing. When the Gospel reached his household, Scripture does not record an order for him to resign from military service.
These accounts are significant for Christians who believe military service can be compatible with discipleship.
But again, silence is not the same as a comprehensive endorsement of every military action.
The Bible does not give us permission to turn a soldier's conversion into approval of unjust warfare.
Nor does it allow us to erase these soldiers from the biblical record because their existence complicates an argument for absolute pacifism.
We must let Scripture speak.
Even when it makes our conclusions harder.
What about Romans 13?
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sword” is μάχαιραν (machairan).
Paul recognizes that governing authorities exercise coercive power and bear responsibility for restraining wrongdoing.
For Christians who affirm the possibility of just military service, Romans 13 contributes to a broader biblical argument that legitimate authorities may sometimes use force to protect society.
But notice something crucial.
Romans 13 follows Romans 12.
And Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath.”
Then Romans 12:21 declares:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
Paul distinguishes personal vengeance from the governing authority's responsibility to administer justice.
Christians disagree about how these teachings apply to believers who personally serve as agents of the state.
Some believe Christians may participate in the state's legitimate protective functions without embracing hatred or revenge.
Others believe disciples must leave coercive violence to the governing authorities rather than personally participate in it.
That disagreement cannot be resolved by pretending either Romans 12 or Romans 13 does not exist.
And there is another important boundary.
Government authority is real.
But it is not absolute.
When the apostles were commanded to stop preaching Jesus, Peter and the others answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29 (KJV)
That principle is unmistakable.
No government possesses the authority to command a Christian to commit what God forbids.
But applying that principle to military service requires careful moral discernment.
It does not automatically prove that all military service is sinful.
Nor does it mean that obeying a military order excuses a Christian from moral responsibility.
An order to deliberately murder civilians, torture prisoners, or commit atrocities does not become righteous simply because a superior issued it.
A uniform cannot wash away sin.
A flag cannot replace the cross.
And loyalty to a nation must never become greater than loyalty to Jesus Christ.
The two Christian convictions that cannot simply be dismissed
Across Christian history, believers have developed two major approaches to this question.
One is often called Christian pacifism or Christian nonviolence.
It emphasizes Jesus' teachings about enemy-love, His refusal to defend His kingdom through violence, His willingness to suffer, and the apostolic instruction not to repay evil for evil.

Many Christians in historic peace-church traditions, including Mennonites, Quakers, and some Anabaptist communities, have understood these teachings as prohibiting their participation in killing during war.
For them, refusing combat is not necessarily refusing to love their country.
It can be an expression of obedience to Christ.
They may serve through medical care, disaster relief, humanitarian work, or other forms of noncombatant service.
The other major approach is often called just-war reasoning.
It recognizes the tragic possibility that force may sometimes be necessary to defend innocent people against aggression.

This tradition, developed extensively in Christian moral theology, argues that the use of force must be constrained by justice, legitimate authority, right intention, necessity, proportionality, and the protection of noncombatants.
It does not teach that every war is justified.
It does not teach that Christians should glorify violence.
And it certainly does not teach that hatred becomes holy when directed against an enemy nation.
Its central concern is that refusing to restrain violent aggression can sometimes leave vulnerable people exposed to terrible harm.
Imagine a soldier who sees armed attackers threatening helpless children.
He intervenes to protect them.
His purpose is not revenge.
His purpose is to save lives.

A Christian who follows just-war reasoning may believe that such protective action can be an expression of love for the victims, even while recognizing the terrible moral weight of using force against the attackers.
A Christian pacifist may respond that the follower of Jesus must seek protection through nonlethal means, courageous intervention, rescue, and sacrificial suffering rather than intentional killing.
These convictions differ profoundly.
But both must face difficult questions.
To the pacifist: How should Christians respond when the innocent face immediate, deadly violence?
To the Christian who accepts military force: How will you ensure that your willingness to fight never becomes hatred, revenge, blind nationalism, or participation in injustice?
Neither question should be treated lightly.
And neither person should assume that sincere disagreement automatically proves the other has abandoned Jesus.
The conscience that refuses to be bought
Now imagine a young Christian receiving an order to report for military service.
He has prayed.
He has studied Scripture.
He has spoken with mature believers.
He has wrestled with the Sermon on the Mount until the words seem engraved upon his soul.
He knows that people will misunderstand him.
He knows that refusing military service may bring legal consequences, depending on his country's laws.
He knows he may lose opportunities, face rejection, or be accused of cowardice.
Yet he cannot escape one conviction:
“I cannot personally participate in killing another human being without violating what I believe Jesus commands me.”
Is he automatically rebelling against God?
No.
A Christian may hold that conviction sincerely and seek conscientious-objector status or lawful noncombatant alternatives.
But sincerity alone does not make every interpretation correct. His conscience must remain open to Scripture, correction, prayer, and wise counsel.
Romans 14:23 says:
“For whatsoever is not of faith is sin.” (KJV)
In context, Paul is addressing disputes over matters such as eating and conscience, not directly discussing military service.
Nevertheless, the passage establishes an important principle: acting against one's sincere conviction before God is spiritually serious.
And Romans 14:12 reminds us:
“So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.”
We should not use these verses to suggest that personal conscience is infallible.
A conscience can be mistaken.
It can be poorly informed.
It can be hardened.
It must be shaped by God's Word.
But a Christian should not be pressured to violate a serious moral conviction simply because someone else finds that conviction inconvenient.

If you are facing compulsory service, seek reliable legal advice about the laws of your jurisdiction and any available conscientious-objector or alternative-service provisions. Christian conviction and legal exemption are related questions, but they are not identical.
And if you are a Christian already serving in the military, this discussion is not a declaration that God has abandoned you.
Your profession does not place you beyond the reach of grace.
Your calling is to examine every part of your life under the lordship of Christ.
The soldier who refuses to hate
Perhaps you are reading this while wearing a military uniform.
Perhaps you have served in combat.
Perhaps you have buried friends.
Perhaps you have witnessed things you still cannot describe without feeling something tighten inside your chest.
And perhaps a question has followed you home:
“Can Jesus still love someone like me?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not a message that Christ saves only those whose past is clean.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every consequence of our failures.
Not after we found the words to explain everything we had done.
While we were yet sinners.
This does not erase moral responsibility.
It does not declare every action committed in war innocent.
Where there has been wrongdoing, repentance matters. Truth matters. Justice matters. Making amends where possible matters.
But neither does the Gospel declare that a person who has participated in war is beyond forgiveness.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The same Lord who called fishermen and tax collectors also received the faith of a Roman centurion.
The same Savior who rebuked Peter's sword also restored Peter after his devastating denial.
And the same Christ who prayed for His enemies on the cross still calls broken people to repentance and new life.
You are not required to pretend your wounds do not exist.
You are not required to call evil good.
You are invited to bring the truth into the presence of the One who died and rose again.
Because grace does not rewrite history by pretending the past never happened. Grace rewrites the future by bringing sinners into reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
That is the heart of our message.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Christian who refuses to carry a weapon must still be willing to carry a cross
There is something that needs to be said to Christians who believe Jesus forbids them from participating in warfare.
Refusing military service does not automatically make a person courageous.
It may be courageous.
It may require extraordinary sacrifice.
But Christian nonviolence is more than refusing to shoot.
Jesus never commanded His followers merely to avoid certain weapons.
He commanded them to love.
And love demands action.
Will you help the wounded?
Will you shelter the displaced?
Will you feed those who have lost everything?
Will you care for the grieving family of someone who fought on the side you oppose?
Will you pray for people who mock your convictions?
Will you risk your comfort to protect vulnerable lives through peaceful means?
Will you serve your neighbors when there is no applause?
Because Christian nonviolence, if it is genuinely rooted in the Gospel, cannot be an excuse for indifference.
And Christian military service, if it is genuinely governed by biblical ethics, cannot become an excuse for cruelty.
Both must answer to Jesus.
The Christian who refuses to fight must not despise the soldier.
The Christian soldier must not despise the conscientious objector.
And neither may use religious language to escape the demands of sacrificial love.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24 (KJV)
Notice what He did not say.
He did not promise that following Him would always make us popular.
He did not promise that everyone would understand our convictions.
He did not promise that obedience would never cost us something.
He called us to follow Him.
Even when the road is difficult.
But here is the question that reaches beyond the battlefield
What if the enemy Jesus is commanding you to love is not a soldier from another nation?
What if it is your father?
The friend who betrayed you?
The person who spread lies about your family?
The neighbor who humiliated you?
The relative whose words still hurt years later?
It is possible to argue passionately about whether Christians should participate in war while quietly nourishing hatred toward someone in our own home.
We can condemn violence on the battlefield while using our tongues to destroy people.
We can quote Matthew 5:44 and still refuse to forgive a brother.
We can preach peace to nations while refusing reconciliation across our own dinner tables.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
If Jesus commands me to love an enemy carrying a weapon, what excuse do I have for refusing to love an enemy carrying only the memory of what they did to me?
That does not mean forgiveness removes accountability.
It does not mean an abused person must return to an unsafe relationship.
It does not mean trust is automatically restored.
Biblical love can coexist with boundaries, justice, and the protection of the vulnerable.
But hatred must not become the ruler of our hearts.
The cross confronts all of us.
The pacifist.
The soldier.
The politician.
The pastor.
The person who has never touched a weapon but has wounded others with words.
We all need mercy.
The cross is where our arguments must finally bow
At Calvary, Jesus was not dying because He had failed to resist Rome.
He was willingly giving His life according to the Father's saving purpose.
He bore our sins.
He fulfilled the Scriptures.
He accomplished what no military victory, political revolution, or human moral achievement could ever accomplish.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
Colossians 1:20 speaks of God making peace through the blood of Christ's cross.
The Greek phrase is:
εἰρηνοποιήσας διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ σταυροῦ αὐτοῦ
Eirēnopoiēsas dia tou haimatos tou staurou autou.
“Having made peace through the blood of his cross.”
This is not merely a message about ending human conflicts.
In context, Paul is proclaiming the cosmic significance of Christ's reconciling work.
Sin has alienated humanity from God.
And peace with God comes through Jesus Christ.
The deepest problem in the human heart cannot be solved by military strength.
But neither can it be solved by merely refusing military service.
A person can be a pacifist and still need salvation.
A person can be a decorated soldier and still need salvation.
A person can possess a flawless public reputation and still need salvation.
Because our greatest need is not simply a new political position.
It is a new heart.
A heart humbled by repentance.
A heart rescued by grace.
A heart transformed through faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than an argument.
It becomes an invitation.
Come to Christ.
Not to defend your image.
Not to prove you are morally superior.
Not to hide behind your uniform or your refusal to wear one.
Come as a sinner in need of mercy.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from sin.
Trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose from the dead.
And allow His Word to reshape the way you think about enemies, nations, justice, courage, forgiveness, and love.
So, can a Christian refuse military service because of Jesus' teaching on loving enemies?
Yes.

A Christian may conscientiously conclude that following Jesus requires refusing combat or military participation, and there are substantial biblical arguments and longstanding Christian traditions supporting that conviction.

But Scripture does not explicitly command every Christian soldier to resign, and other Christians, seeking to obey the same Lord, conclude that morally constrained military service may be permissible when directed toward the just protection of others.
The existence of sincere disagreement does not make every action morally acceptable.
Aggression, atrocities, revenge, cruelty, and the deliberate targeting of innocent people cannot be sanctified by patriotic language.
And neither position should be embraced merely because it is convenient.
The Christian must study Scripture faithfully, seek wisdom humbly, obey God above human authorities, and remain willing to bear the cost of conviction.
Above all, the Christian must refuse to surrender the command of Jesus to love.
Because whether you carry a weapon or refuse one, you cannot faithfully follow Christ while celebrating hatred.
And perhaps that is the question we should carry away from this discussion.
Not simply:
“Would I be willing to die for my country?”
But also:
“Am I willing to surrender my pride, my hatred, my revenge, and even my reputation in order to obey Jesus?”
That is where discipleship becomes real.
That is where faith stops being a slogan.
And that is where the cross exposes the difference between admiring Jesus and actually following Him.
If this message has unsettled something inside you, do not rush past it.
Bring that conviction before God.
Pray over the Scriptures.
Speak with mature believers who will help you seek truth rather than simply reinforce your opinions.

And if you believe Christians can disagree on this issue while remaining faithful to Christ, share your understanding respectfully. Let the conversation be governed by Scripture, humility, and love—not insults.
Someone reading your testimony may be carrying a question they have never dared to ask out loud.
Someone may need to know that struggling with a difficult moral question does not mean they must stop seeking Jesus.
And someone may need to hear that forgiveness is still possible.
We are not here to build a community that merely wins religious arguments.
We want to help people know Jesus Christ, understand His Word, repent of sin, receive His grace, and grow into mature disciples who live what they believe.
For those who have been praying about how to support Gospel-centered work, this can be one meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.
Scripture teaches that believers may support those who minister the Word, as reflected in Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14. It also teaches that giving should be willing rather than coerced.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
God is glorified through faith in Christ, obedience, love, truth, worship, generosity, and faithful service.
These resources are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
Pray for this ministry.
Help another person open the Bible.
Speak about Jesus with someone who has lost hope.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by payments, purchases, or religious performance.
And that grace is exactly why we want the message to keep reaching people.
Because somewhere there may be a young believer staring at a military summons, frightened by the possibility of choosing between conscience and country.
Somewhere there may be a soldier who cannot sleep because of what he has seen.
Somewhere there may be a family praying for someone serving in a dangerous place.
Somewhere there may be a person who has spent years believing that what happened in war placed them beyond God's mercy.
And somewhere there may be a person who has never faced a battlefield but has spent a lifetime fighting a war of bitterness within their own heart.
All of them need more than an argument.
They need truth.
They need grace.
They need the Savior.
The final question is not whether you have always made the right decision.
None of us has.
The final question is whether you will bring your life, your conscience, your sins, your wounds, and your future under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the kingdom of God is not advanced by hatred.
And the peace that matters most cannot be manufactured by human power.
It was purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
You may never be called to lay down a weapon—but every follower of Jesus will be called to lay down something at the foot of the cross.
